(i) Both are metallic, but Mg²⁺ has a higher charge and is smaller than Na⁺, and each Mg atom releases two delocalized electrons, so the electrostatic attraction between cations and delocalized electrons is stronger (greater charge density).

(ii) Silicon is a covalent network (giant/macromolecular) structure: many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.

(iii) P4, Cl2 and Ar exist as small discrete molecules/atoms held only by weak London (dispersion) forces, which need little energy to overcome.

(iv) S8 molecules are larger than P4 (more electrons), so the London forces between them are stronger.

(i) Both have metallic bonding. Mg has more delocalized electrons (2 vs 1) and a smaller, more highly charged ion (Mg2+), so the attraction between cations and delocalized electrons is stronger → higher m.p.

(ii) Silicon is a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure; many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.

(iii) Both have only weak London (dispersion) forces; Cl2 has more electrons/larger molar mass than Ar, so stronger forces and higher m.p.

• Sulfur is a simple molecular (S8) covalent substance;
  • all outer electrons are held in covalent bonds/lone pairs – no delocalized electrons or ions, so it does not conduct;
  • aluminium is a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalized electrons;
  • these delocalized electrons move when a potential difference is applied → good conductor.

(i) Any three: Mg has twice as many delocalized electrons per atom; Mg2+ has a greater charge; and is smaller than Na+; so the attraction between cations and delocalized electrons is stronger in Mg (higher m.p.).

(ii) MgO is a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attraction between Mg2+ and O2−; SO2 is simple molecular with only weak intermolecular (London/dipole–dipole) forces. Ionic bonding is much stronger, so MgO melts at a much higher temperature.

(i) Mg has a greater ionic charge (Mg2+ vs Na+) and more delocalized electrons per atom (2 vs 1). This gives a stronger attraction between the cations and the delocalized electrons, so the metallic bonding is stronger.

(ii) Si has a giant covalent (network) structure, and many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.

(iii) P4, S8, Cl2 and Ar are simple molecular substances. Only weak London (dispersion) forces between molecules must be overcome. “Weak intermolecular forces” alone is not enough.

• From Na+ to Mg2+ to Al3+ the cation charge increases and the radius decreases (higher charge density), and more electrons are delocalized per atom…
  • …so the electrostatic attraction between the cations and the sea of delocalized electrons increases, giving stronger metallic bonding. ("Increasing nuclear charge" alone and "cloud of electrons" are not accepted.)

Bonding: metallic bonding, the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive ions and a sea of delocalized electrons (2 marks max).

Conductivity: the delocalized electrons are free to move through the structure when a voltage is applied.

Malleability: the layers of cations can slide past each other without breaking the bonding, because the electron sea still holds them together.

(i) Conductivity: metals have a sea of delocalized electrons that are mobile and carry charge. Malleability: layers of positive ions (cations) can slide past each other without breaking the metallic bond (not "nuclei").

(ii) Co3+ = [Ar]3d6: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p boxes all filled with paired arrows; 4s empty; 3d: one box paired, four boxes with single parallel arrows.

(iii) Co2+ (cobalt(II)).

(iv) [3 max] Co3+ has a partially filled 3d sub-level; the NH3 ligands split the d orbitals into two sets of different energy; electrons absorb certain frequencies of visible light to move from lower to higher d orbitals; the complementary (remaining) colour is seen.

(i) A lattice of Mg2+ cations surrounded by a sea of delocalized electrons; bonding is the electrostatic attraction between them.

(ii) Mg contributes two delocalized electrons per atom (Mg2+ vs Na+), so the metallic bonding is stronger.

(iii) The different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other as easily.
Any two, e.g.: V2O5 in the Contact process (2SO2 + O2 → 2SO3); Fe in the Haber process (N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3); Ni/Pd/Pt in hydrogenation of alkenes (margarine); Pt/Pd/Rh in catalytic converters.
Electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive ions (cations) and a sea of delocalized electrons. Writing 'metallic bonding' alone scores no marks.

(i) 4s: one box with ↑. 3d: five boxes, each with ↑. Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹, with six unpaired electrons. The sublevels must be labelled.

(ii) Electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalized electrons.

(iii) Layers of cations can slide past each other without breaking the metallic bond, because the delocalized electrons move with them.
Metallic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions (cations) and a sea of delocalized electrons.

(i) Any two: Ca has stronger metallic bonding; Ca has a smaller atomic/ionic radius (more closely packed); Ca delocalizes two electrons per atom/has a 2+ ion; Ca has a greater atomic mass (40.08 vs 39.10).

(ii) It has delocalized (mobile) electrons that are free to move through the lattice and carry charge.
Both Fe2+ ([Ar]3d6) and Fe3+ ([Ar]3d5) are paramagnetic, because they contain unpaired electrons in their d orbitals (attracted into a magnetic field).
Metallic bonding: electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive iron ions (cations) and a sea of delocalized electrons.
Layers of Al3+ ions can slide over each other without breaking the bonding, because the delocalized electrons keep attracting the cations (metallic bonding is non-directional).
